LLM: Large Language Model — a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language, the basis of systems like GPT and Claude.
MLLM: Multimodal Large Language Model — an LLM extended to also take images, video, or audio as input, not just text.
SFT: Supervised Fine-Tuning — training a pretrained model further on labeled examples of the exact task you want it to do.
RL: Reinforcement Learning — training a model by rewarding good actions and penalizing bad ones, rather than showing it labeled examples directly.
RLHF: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — using human preference ratings as the reward signal to fine-tune a model's behavior.
DPO: Direct Preference Optimization — a way to fine-tune a model on human preference data without needing a separate reward model, simpler than RLHF.
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — a model looks up relevant documents at answer-time and uses them as context, instead of relying only on what it memorized during training.
Gaussian Splatting: A technique for representing and rendering 3D scenes as a cloud of small blob-like "splats" instead of a mesh or neural field, popular for fast, realistic 3D reconstruction.
JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture — a model design that predicts a target's embedding (compressed representation) rather than the target's raw pixels or tokens, meant to be more efficient to train.
MPC: Model Predictive Control — a control method that repeatedly plans a short sequence of future actions using a model of how the system behaves, then takes just the first action and re-plans.
Quantization: Compressing a model by storing its weights with fewer bits (e.g. 4-bit instead of 16-bit), which shrinks memory and speeds up inference at some cost to accuracy.
PTX: NVIDIA's intermediate, near-assembly instruction format for GPU code — writing or generating PTX directly gives fine control over how a kernel actually runs on the hardware.
CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — the standard public ID system for tracking known software security flaws (e.g. "CVE-2026-12345").
DoS: Denial-of-Service — an attack that overwhelms a system so it can't serve legitimate requests, rather than trying to steal data.
SMT solver: Satisfiability Modulo Theories solver — software that automatically checks whether a set of logical/mathematical constraints can be satisfied, used inside many reasoning and verification systems.
jailbreak: A prompt or technique designed to get an AI model to bypass its safety guidelines and produce output it was trained to refuse.
UQ: Uncertainty Quantification — measuring how confident a model actually is in a given prediction, rather than treating every output as equally reliable.
retrosynthesis: In chemistry, working backward from a target molecule to figure out a sequence of reactions that could synthesize it.
diffusion model: A generative model that creates images (or other data) by learning to reverse a process of gradually adding noise, starting from pure noise and denoising it step by step into a final output.
knowledge poisoning: Deliberately inserting false or misleading information into a model's data sources (e.g. documents a RAG system retrieves from) so the model produces incorrect or manipulated answers.
MoE: Mixture-of-Experts — a model architecture that routes each input to a small subset of specialized "expert" sub-networks instead of using the whole model every time, cutting compute cost as models scale up.
MCP: Model Context Protocol — a standard way for AI agents to connect to external tools and data sources (files, APIs, databases) through a common interface, instead of each app building its own custom integration.
CI/CD: Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment — the automated pipeline that builds, tests, and ships code changes, a high-value target for attackers since compromising it can taint everything it deploys.
red team: A group (human or, increasingly, AI-driven) that deliberately attacks a system the way a real adversary would, to find exploitable weaknesses before one does.
vibe coding: Writing software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an AI agent generate and run the code, rather than writing it by hand line by line.
supply chain attack: Compromising a widely-used dependency, package, or build tool so the attack spreads to everyone who installs or builds with it, instead of attacking each victim directly.
